newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cricket - Rixon urges patience after test loss.
newsitem.headline: Cricket - Rixon urges patience after test loss.

text.p: WELLINGTON, Feb 11 - Be patient; that's New Zealand cricket coach Steve Rixon's advice as his team searches for a winning formula in their home international season, NZPA reports.
After just hanging on for a draw in the first test against England at Auckland last month, the Kiwis tumbled to an embarrassing innings and 68-run defeat at the Basin Reserve yesterday.
They were effectively outplayed from start to finish and Rixon is aware that there is a need to quickly follow up the pre-Christmas success in Pakistan, where the test series was drawn 1-1.
"The guys are trying, we've got to be a little patient," Rixon said last night.
"We're not throwing in the towel. We'll be there throwing punches in the last test."
However there was a significant gulf between the two team's performances at the Basin Reserve.
England batted with more thought and skill, bowled tightly and with penetration, and fielded energetically and caught everything on offer.
Rixon admitted New Zealand had been well beaten in the second test.
"We haven't remotely gone close to our best," he said.
"I'd like to think that'll be in Christchurch. If we do that and draw the test series we'll go into the one-day series in a positive frame of mind."
"We've got to lift ourselves and start afresh tomorrow. Christchurch is important to the rest of our season."
The biggest concern for Rixon is the New Zealand batting, which was lacking in commitment and technique against the swinging ball.
That weakness was exploited by England's fast-medium pair Darren Gough and Andrew Caddick, who shared 15 New Zealand wickets between them.

Gough followed his first innings five for 40 with four for 52 in the second, while Caddick, who bowled just as effectively but without quite the same results, completed a highly satisfying return to test cricket with four for 45 and two for 40.
Twelve of New Zealand's 20 wickets in the test were to catches in the arc between wicketkeeper Alec Stewart and gully.
Stewart picked up six catches while second slip Nick Knight, who must rate among the world's best slip fielders, took four in the match.
"We tend to go sparring at balls quite regularly," Rixon said.
"It's a confidence factor. When your confidence goes there's a little hesitancy and anxiety."
However Rixon is unwilling to shackle his batsmen, pointing out the middle order players, notably Stephen Fleming, Nathan Astle and Chris Cairns, are at their best producing positive strokeplay.
"It's the nature of the beast. They are strokeplayers and I don't want to take that strokemaking and individuality out. They're the same players that will win us a test," he said.
While New Zealand have plenty to ponder in the three-day break before the start of the final test at Lancaster Park on Friday, England are bubbling with confidence.
They believe they could have won all four tests played so far on their tour of Zimbabwe and New Zealand with some luck.
They finally struck gold yesterday and will be hard to topple in Christchurch.
"It's nice to finally finish it off," captain Mike Atherton said yesterday.
"I'm very pleased for the players. They've worked hard. We've played good (test) cricket this winter and we deserved to get the victory today."
Atherton was always confident New Zealand's tailend batsmen wouldn't be able to emulate Danny Morrison's achievement in batting 165 minutes to save the first test in Auckland.

"They could hang around in Auckland because it was a dead wicket. There was no way, given a reasonably new ball and bowlers bowling well, that the tailenders were going to hang around any length of time here."
Atherton believed England got their reward for producing consistently solid test cricket on their tour.
"The most important thing is how you perform. In the longer form of the game our performances have been good and sooner or later you'll win games and things finally turned for us today.
"If we keep performing consistently well we'll win more games than we lose."
Now Atherton's intent on not letting the initiative slip, and he insisted there won't be a negative thought going into the final test.
"To win a three-match series generally you've got to win two games so we're going to Christchurch to win that one."
